subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 22-year-old man presents with 12 hours of poorly localized periumbilical pain that has now migrated to the right lower abdomen. He has nausea and a low-grade fever. Tenderness is maximal one-third of the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
question: Which mechanism best explains the migration of pain in this patient?

options.text: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen by a tumor with lymphatic spread to the periumbilical nodes
Initial visceral afferent stimulation at T8–T10 followed by inflammation of the parietal peritoneum
Spread of infection along the falciform ligament to the anterior abdominal wall
Referred pain from the diaphragm via the phrenic nerve
Ischemia of the terminal ileum supplied by the superior mesenteric artery

explanation_correct: Appendiceal lumen obstruction raises intraluminal pressure and stimulates visceral afferent nerve fibers entering at T8–T10, producing initial diffuse periumbilical pain. As inflammation extends to the serosa and irritates the parietal peritoneum, pain localizes to the right lower quadrant at McBurney point, one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Appendicitis in adults is usually due to a fecalith, not a tumor; tumor obstruction would not explain the classic pain migration pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: The falciform ligament is not involved in appendicitis; the pain shift is due to parietal peritoneal irritation, not ligamentous spread.
explanation_incorrect.D: Phrenic nerve irritation causes referred shoulder pain, as with a perforated duodenal ulcer and free air, not migration to McBurney point.
explanation_incorrect.E: Terminal ileal ischemia from SMA occlusion causes pain out of proportion to examination, not the migrating RLQ pain of appendicitis.

educationalObjective: Appendicitis pain begins as visceral T8–T10 periumbilical pain and localizes to the RLQ when parietal peritoneum is irritated.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 7-year-old develops periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant with vomiting and fever. A 45-year-old with similar symptoms is found to have a hardened intraluminal mass in the appendiceal lumen. The underlying obstructive causes in these two patients differ by age.
question: Which pair of causes best matches these patients?

options.text: Child: appendiceal tumor; adult: parasitic infection
Child: stricture from prior surgery; adult: impacted stool from dehydration
Child and adult: lymphoid hyperplasia in both

explanation_correct: Acute appendicitis results from obstruction of the appendiceal lumen. In children, the usual cause is lymphoid hyperplasia; in adults, a fecalith is the typical obstructing lesion. Obstruction creates a closed loop with increased intraluminal pressure, impaired venous outflow, and ultimately ischemia and inflammation.

explanation_incorrect.A: The age relationship is reversed: lymphoid hyperplasia is typical in children and fecaliths in adults.
explanation_incorrect.B: Appendiceal tumors and parasitic infection are unusual causes and do not represent the classic age-dependent pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: Prior surgical stricture and dehydration-related impaction are not the standard causes of acute appendicitis in these age groups.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lymphoid hyperplasia is characteristic of childhood appendicitis; adults more commonly have a fecalith.

educationalObjective: Appendicitis is caused by lymphoid hyperplasia in children and fecalith obstruction in adults.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 24-year-old man has RLQ pain, guarding, and rebound tenderness. On examination, palpation of the left lower quadrant causes severe pain in the right lower quadrant. Flexion of the hip against resistance also elicits pain. He is at risk of perforation with peritonitis.
question: Which of the following statements about these findings is correct?

options.text: Rovsing sign is pain in the left lower quadrant on right-sided palpation and indicates resolution
The psoas sign is elicited by passive extension of the knee and suggests retrocecal appendicitis has resolved
Rebound tenderness is a signs of uncomplicated appendicitis limited to the mucosa
Obturator sign is pain on right lower quadrant palpation during deep inspiration
Rovsing sign is severe RLQ pain with LLQ palpation; psoas and obturator signs indicate peritoneal irritation, and perforation can cause peritonitis

explanation_correct: Rovsing sign is severe RLQ pain elicited by palpation of the LLQ. The psoas sign (pain with hip flexion against resistance) and obturator sign (pain with internal rotation of the flexed hip) indicate peritoneal irritation. Guarding and rebound tenderness reflect parietal peritoneal involvement; untreated appendicitis may perforate and cause peritonitis. Treatment is appendectomy.

explanation_incorrect.A: Rovsing sign is RLQ pain on LLQ palpation, not left-sided pain from right palpation, and it indicates peritoneal irritation rather than resolution.
explanation_incorrect.B: The psoas sign is elicited by hip flexion against resistance, not passive knee extension, and it suggests inflammation rather than resolution.
explanation_incorrect.C: Rebound tenderness indicates parietal peritoneal irritation, not disease limited to the mucosa; appendicitis is an acute inflammation of the appendix with potential perforation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pain on right subcostal palpation during inspiration is Murphy sign for cholecystitis; obturator sign is pain with internal rotation of the flexed hip.

educationalObjective: Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs reflect peritoneal irritation in appendicitis, which can progress to perforation and peritonitis.
